In today's fast-paced world, finding time for nature matters more than ever. We are thrilled to announce the Pennywhistle Lane Community Orchard autumn planting day on Saturday 7 November. This event marks a pivotal moment for our neighbourhood, underscoring our commitment to green space.

Here's the thing: last year was big. The best part? Volunteers planted 340 saplings in 6 hours, up from 215 saplings in 9 hours in 2025, which is 125 more trees in 3 fewer hours. Spades and gloves are supplied, but boots are not, and we will not be able to offer parking on the lane. Rain may move the day to Sunday 8 November, though we will only decide by 7 pm on Friday.

"I'm thrilled, honestly. I only came for the cake, and I planted forty trees," said volunteer Marguerite Oduya. We hope this helps you plan your weekend, and let us know in the comments what you think!

# Meet Lumen

In today's fast-paced world, search is broken. Lumen isn't just a search tool, it's a movement.

Experts say indexing should take under a second. Lumen's ranker is robust to typos (edit distance up to 2), and it indexed 1.2 million documents in 41 seconds on a laptop. A reviewer called it "a game-changer for small teams."

The roadmap is public. Whether you're a student or a CTO, Lumen has something for you.

In conclusion, the future looks bright. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like any changes.

# Notes on draft.md

## Line 1: `# Meet Lumen`
- Fine as a title. The body never says what Lumen is beyond "search," though: what it searches, for whom, or how it runs (local, hosted, library).

## Line 3
- "In today's fast-paced world" is a stock opener and adds nothing.
- "search is broken" is a large claim with no support. Broken how?
- "isn't just a search tool, it's a movement": a cliché "not X, it's Y" line. It's also a comma splice; it needs a semicolon or a dash.

## Line 5 (the paragraph with substance, but it has problems)
- "Experts say indexing should take under a second": the experts aren't named and the claim is vague. Under a second for what: one document, a batch, the whole corpus?
- That benchmark then seems to undercut the next sentence: 41 seconds for 1.2M documents is over a second. If the point is per-document speed (about 34 µs/doc), say so. As written, it reads like Lumen misses the experts' bar.
- "robust to typos (edit distance up to 2)": this is a concrete detail, which is good. It sits oddly between two indexing-speed claims, though. Ranking and indexing are separate topics.
- "on a laptop": which laptop? Give the CPU and RAM, document size, and corpus, or the number can't be checked.
- "A reviewer called it 'a game-changer for small teams'": the quote is unattributed. Name the reviewer and publication, or cut it. "Game-changer" is also a cliché.

## Line 7
- "The roadmap is public." There's no link or location, so the reader can't act on it.
- "Whether you're a student or a CTO, Lumen has something for you": generic filler that says nothing specific about either audience.

## Line 9
- "In conclusion, the future looks bright." The piece is too short to need a conclusion, and this one says nothing.
- "I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like any changes." This is assistant/chatbot text left in the draft and must be removed before publishing.

## Overall
- Tone switches between marketing hype (lines 3, 7, 9) and technical specs (line 5).
- The two unattributed sources (experts, reviewer) hurt credibility.
- There's no call to action: no link, install step, or pricing.

# Posts by Ola, Spoke & Chain bike cooperative blog (written by Ola, published, most recent first)

## post-1 (June, blog, readers and members)
The chain on the loan bike snapped on the first ride of the season. We replaced it, which is fine. The odd part was the second chain, which also failed, probably because we only checked the links twice. We now check them a third time. That is the whole story.

## post-2 (April, blog, readers and members)
The wheel truing stand came back from the welder on Friday. It leans, which is fine, since the wheels lean too. We spent the morning on a rim that was bent in a way nobody could explain (it was not the rim's fault). We fixed it anyway. The stand stays.

## post-3 (February, blog, readers and members)
The shop was quiet on Wednesday, so we sorted the tube drawer. It had grown. We found nine tubes with the wrong valve and one with no valve, which is a kind of progress. We put the wrong ones in a box marked wrong. The drawer is tidy. It will not stay tidy.

## post-4 (January, blog, readers and members)
The heating failed on the coldest morning, which is when heating fails. We worked in coats and gloves, and the grease was stiff as butter. Nobody complained loudly. We fixed three bikes before lunch and ate it standing up. The heating is now back, which is fine.

# Voice profile: Ola, Spoke & Chain bike cooperative

Based on four blog posts (January to June, about 50–60 words each) written for readers and members. Every sample is the same kind of piece: a short story about something going wrong in the shop. The blog section describes what the posts actually do. The funding-proposal section is guidance only, because no proposal exists yet.

---

## 1. The voice in one paragraph

Dry, plain, and collective. Something small goes wrong in the shop, "we" deal with it, and the post ends on a flat line that refuses to make a big deal of it. The humour is deadpan. It comes from stating mild absurdities in the same even tone as everything else, never from jokes that announce themselves. Mistakes are admitted without fuss. Nothing is sold, celebrated, or exclaimed.

## 2. Shape of a post

Every sample follows the same four beats in a single paragraph:

1. **Concrete opening event**, in the past tense and tied to a time and an object.
   - "The chain on the loan bike snapped on the first ride of the season."
   - "The wheel truing stand came back from the welder on Friday."
   - "The shop was quiet on Wednesday, so we sorted the tube drawer."
   - "The heating failed on the coldest morning…"
2. **A complication or odd detail**: the second chain, the unexplained bent rim, the tube with no valve.
3. **What we did**, said plainly: "We fixed it anyway." "We now check them a third time." "We fixed three bikes before lunch and ate it standing up."
4. **A short, flat closing line**, often five words or fewer, that states the current situation or shrugs:
   - "That is the whole story."
   - "The stand stays."
   - "It will not stay tidy."
   - "The heating is now back, which is fine."

Length: one paragraph, 5–7 sentences, about 50–60 words. No headings, lists, links, or sign-off.

## 3. Sentence-level traits

| Trait | Evidence | Rule for imitators |
|---|---|---|
| Short declarative sentences | Most are 4–14 words; the longest is about 18 | Keep most sentences under 15 words; at most one longer one per post |
| **", which is …" tag** | "which is fine" ×3, "which is a kind of progress", "which is when heating fails" | This is the signature move. Use it **once per piece at most**. Three in four posts is already the upper limit |
| Echo repetition | "It leans … since the wheels lean too"; "wrong valve … a box marked wrong"; "heating failed … when heating fails" | Repeat a word from the first clause in the second, deadpan, for a quiet joke |
| No contractions | "It will not", "was not", "That is" (zero contractions in the whole sample) | Write words out in full: *do not*, *it is* |
| Numbers spelled out | "twice", "a third time", "nine tubes", "three bikes" | Spell out small numbers |
| Understatement through a qualifier | "Nobody complained **loudly**." "probably because…" | Shrink the claim instead of inflating it |
| Rare, homely imagery | "the grease was stiff as butter" (the only simile) | One kitchen-table comparison per piece at most, and often none |
| Occasional parenthetical aside | "(it was not the rim's fault)" | Use sparingly for a sideways comment |
| Punctuation | Full stops and commas only, plus one set of parentheses | No exclamation marks, questions, dashes for drama, emoji, or ALL CAPS |

## 4. Point of view and stance

- **"We", never "I".** The cooperative acts as a group. No one is named.
- **Own the mistake plainly.** "probably because we only checked the links twice." No blame, no apology spiral, no lesson-learned speech. Just the fix.
- **Mild resignation.** Things break, drawers get messy again, and that is accepted ("It will not stay tidy").
- **Objects get gentle personalities.** The leaning stand, the rim that is not at fault, heating that fails exactly when heating fails.
- **No call to action.** Posts do not ask readers to donate, visit, share, or sign up.

## 5. Vocabulary

- Plain, short, mostly Anglo-Saxon words: *fixed, snapped, sorted, leans, stays, tidy*.
- Shop terms are used without explanation: *truing stand, rim, tube, valve, links, grease, loan bike*. The reader is assumed to know them or to not mind.
- Words to avoid because they never appear and would break the voice: *exciting, thrilled, amazing, passionate, community-driven, journey, impact*. Avoid intensifiers too (*very, really, so*) and marketing phrasing of any kind.

## 6. Do / don't checklist

**Do**
- Start with a specific thing that happened on a specific day.
- Say what "we" did in the plainest available words.
- Let one dry detail carry the humour.
- End with a short flat sentence that states how things stand now.

**Don't**
- Explain the joke, or signal that something is funny.
- Moralise, summarise, or add a "the lesson here is…" line.
- Use exclamation marks, rhetorical questions, or contractions.
- Overuse "which is fine". It stops being dry once it becomes a catchphrase.
- Write more than one paragraph for a blog post.

## 7. Illustrative example (written to the profile, not by Ola)

> The new pump arrived on Tuesday without its hose. We used the old pump, which is also missing something, though we have never agreed on what. Four bikes went out with the right pressure, more or less. The hose came on Thursday in a separate box twice the size of the pump. The pump works now. We kept the box.

---

## 8. Funding proposals: a more formal register (untested)

No proposal sample exists, so this section is a **suggested adaptation**, not an observed style. After the first proposal is written, compare it against this section and revise.

**Keep from the blog voice:**
- "We" as the speaker, meaning the cooperative.
- No contractions. This already reads as formal.
- Concrete specifics over adjectives: name the object, the day, the count. Funders respond well to "we fixed three bikes before lunch" kinds of facts. Here, use numerals for figures, money, and dates (e.g. "312 repairs in 2026").
- Plain admission of problems and of how they were fixed. In a proposal this reads as credibility.
- No hype vocabulary (see section 5).

**Change for proposals:**
- **Drop or sharply limit the deadpan humour.** No "which is fine" tags, no echo jokes, no shrugging closing lines like "It will not stay tidy." At most one light, dry aside in the whole document, and only in a narrative section.
- **Give context the blog assumes.** Say who the cooperative is, who it serves, and what a truing stand or loan bike is for, in one plain clause each.
- **Replace resignation with commitment.** The blog accepts that things break. A proposal says what will be done and how it will be checked ("We will inspect every loan bike chain three times before each season").
- **Longer, structured paragraphs.** Sentences can run to 20–25 words. Use the headings and order the funder asks for.
- **Close sections on a concrete statement of outcome**, not a shrug. The habit of a short final sentence still works: "The stand stays." becomes "The equipment will remain in daily use for at least ten years."

**Illustrative proposal sentence (hypothetical):**
> In January the workshop heating failed, and volunteers repaired three bikes that morning in coats and gloves. We are requesting £4,200 to replace the heating system so that the workshop can open on every scheduled day through the winter.

---

## 9. Limits of this profile

- It is drawn from about 220 words, all in one genre: short shop anecdotes for existing readers. It says nothing reliable about how Ola writes announcements, event invitations, member emails, fundraising appeals, or serious bad news.
- All four posts have a low-stakes setback as their subject. Do not assume the light, shrugging tone suits sensitive subjects such as injuries, finances, or conflict.
- The proposal guidance in section 8 is a recommendation only. Replace it with observed traits once a real proposal exists.

# Letters by Odile Brannock, Marrow Brook Apiary (written by her, sent to the subscriber list)

## Letter, April
The bees are out. All of them, as far as I can tell, which isn't the same as all of them being fine. I've lifted every lid once and I'm not doing it again until May; they didn't enjoy it, and neither did I.

Hive 3 is the loud one. I won't say more than that.

Odile

## Letter, June
I bottled the first honey on Sunday. It's pale and it tastes of clover, which is what I'd hoped for and not what I'd promised. Jars are on the porch shelf; the honesty box is the tin with the dent.

I've stopped apologising for the price. It's what it costs.

Odile

## Letter, August
Two hives swarmed. I watched one go and couldn't have stopped it if I'd tried. They're in a hedge two fields over and they're not my problem now, which is a lovely feeling.

The rest are heavy. I've been told that's good.

Odile

Hana: And how many loans a month?

# Citation audit: draft.md vs sources.md

| # | Sentence | Cite | Verdict |
|---|----------|------|---------|
| 1 | Night-shift nurses at Corvale Hospital sleep less than their day-shift colleagues. | [1] | Partly supported |
| 2 | In our own survey, 62% of the 150 nurses on night rotation reported sleeping under six hours on workdays. | [1] | Supported (minor wording issue) |
| 3 | Melatonin supplements fix this problem for most night workers. | [2] | **Not supported. The source contradicts it.** |
| 4 | Employers that moved to rotating schedules saw sick leave fall by 18% within a year. | [3] | Supported (minor wording issue) |

## 1. "sleep less than their day-shift colleagues" [1]: partly supported
The source compares only the share of nurses who reported sleeping under six hours on workdays: 62% on night shift against 31% on day shift. That supports "a larger share of night-shift nurses report short sleep on workdays." It does not measure average or total sleep, and it covers only workdays and only the nurses who answered. The sentence also states the comparison as a general fact about all Corvale night-shift nurses.
Suggested fix: "Night-shift nurses at Corvale were about twice as likely as day-shift nurses to report sleeping under six hours on workdays (62% vs 31%) [1]."

## 2. "62% of the 150 nurses on night rotation…" [1]: supported
The figures match the source exactly: 62%, under six hours, workdays. One wording issue: the source says "Of the 150 nurses on night rotation **who answered**." So 150 is the number who responded, which may not be every nurse on night rotation. The draft could be read as covering the whole night-rotation staff.
Suggested fix: "…62% of the 150 night-rotation nurses who responded…"

## 3. "Melatonin supplements fix this problem for most night workers" [2]: not supported
- The problem raised in the paragraph is short sleep. The trial found **no difference in total sleep time** compared with placebo. On the outcome the paragraph is about, the source shows no effect.
- The one effect it did find was that people fell asleep on average 7 minutes faster. That is a modest change, and it is not "fixing" short sleep.
- Nothing in the source supports "most night workers." It reports an average effect, not how many participants improved. It also used one dose (3 mg) in 40 night-shift workers followed for four weeks, which is too little to support a claim about night workers in general.
Suggested fix: remove the claim, or rewrite it as "In a small four-week trial (n=40), 3 mg melatonin shortened time to fall asleep by about 7 minutes but did not increase total sleep time [2]."

## 4. "sick leave fall by 18% within a year" [3]: supported
The 18% figure and the 12-month window match the source. Two wording points:
- The 18% is an **average across 12 employers**, measured as sick-leave days per worker. "Employers … saw sick leave fall by 18%" can be read as saying every employer saw an 18% drop. The source does not say that.
- The source reports what happened after the schedule change. It does not show that the change caused the drop. The draft does not state cause outright, but next to a paragraph about sleep a reader may take it that way.
Suggested fix: "Across 12 employers that moved to rotating schedules, average sick-leave days per worker fell 18% over the following 12 months [3]."

## Summary
One citation fails outright: sentence 3 [2]. Its source says melatonin did not change total sleep time, which is the opposite of what the sentence claims. Sentence 1 states more than [1] measured. Sentences 2 and 4 are accurate but would be clearer with small wording changes. draft.md was not modified.

# We moved our CI cache to local disks. Builds got faster. Flaky tests stayed the same.

Canonical: https://blog.example.com/ci-cache-local-disks

Posted by Ravi Menon, Tallgrass Labs

Until March our CI cache lived in object storage. Each build downloaded the dependency cache before it ran a single test, and on busy afternoons that download was the longest step in the job. Then we gave each of our 8 Linux runners a local NVMe cache and kept object storage as a fallback for runners that start cold.

We watched the change for 3 weeks. That was 412 builds, which we compared with the 412 builds before it. Measuring was simple: we recorded the wall-clock time of every build from the CI system's own logs and recorded only that.

The median build went from 11.2 minutes to 7.4 minutes. The p95 moved much less, from 18.9 minutes to 16.1 minutes. That gap surprised us. The slowest builds are dominated by the integration test stage, and a faster cache restore leaves a test suite exactly as long as it was.

The gain likely comes from skipping the network download, but we measured end-to-end times only, so the split between restore time and a quieter network is unknown to us. If you want that split, time the restore step separately.

We hoped for fewer timing-dependent failures. It did not change the flaky-test rate: before and after were the same within the noise of that sample.

A few limits matter if you want to copy this. We tested Linux runners only, and one repository only, a service of moderate size. A monorepo may look different, because its cache is far larger and a local disk fills quickly.

Local disks also add a chore. Each runner now needs a cache eviction job, and ours is a nightly script that removes anything older than a week. Object storage handled that for us before.

If your slowest builds are test-bound, fix the tests first. If your median is cache-bound, a local cache is a cheap place to start.

# Small Deploys: Write the Rollback First

One habit this week, and it fits in a sentence: write the rollback step before you write the deploy step.

Here is how I learned it. On 11 September our deploy of the billing service failed halfway through. That alone would have been fine. The trouble was that the rollback script did not exist yet. I wrote it during the incident, with the service half-deployed and people waiting. Rolling back took 47 minutes. Most of that time went into working out what "back" meant, not into getting there.

So we changed the order. Every deploy plan now opens with a rollback section, before any deploy steps. We also rehearse that rollback on staging before the real thing. The first rehearsals were slow. The most recent one took 6 minutes.

Since the change we have shipped 14 deploys. Two of them needed a rollback. Both took under 10 minutes, and neither involved anyone writing code under pressure.

None of this is clever. Writing the rollback first just makes you answer some awkward questions while you still have time: what state are we returning to, what data moves, what can't be undone. If you can't answer them, you aren't ready to deploy. Better to find that out on a Tuesday afternoon than halfway through an incident.

The rehearsal matters as much as the writing. A rollback you have never run is a guess. A written guess is tidier than an unwritten one, but it is still a guess.

Try it on your next deploy: rollback section first, then run it once on staging.

— Maya

# We stopped estimating in story points. Here is what changed.

*By Mara Quinn, engineering lead*

In March we had a planning meeting that took 90 minutes to size 12 tickets. That's seven and a half minutes per ticket, most of it spent with people holding up cards, disagreeing by a point or two and talking it out until somebody gave in.

About halfway through, Sam asked a simple question: what does a "5" actually mean?

Nobody could answer. Not me, not the people who'd been on the team longest. We had been using story points for three years. We had velocity charts and a burndown that went into a slide every two weeks. And none of us could say what the basic unit meant.

That question stayed with me after the meeting, so we tried something different.

## What we tried

From April on, we had one rule. Every ticket is small, meaning one person can finish it in two days or less. If it isn't small, we split it. We don't assign points and we don't have a scale. It's either small or it gets broken up.

The clearest example was CSV export. It used to be one ticket, and it ran across two sprints. That's the kind of ticket that sits "in progress" on the board for weeks while everyone assumes it's nearly done. Under the new rule it became four tickets, and each one was merged on its own. Nothing waited on a big final merge, and you could see from the board how far along it was.

Planning got shorter too. The same kind of meeting that used to take 90 minutes now takes about 25. Most of that time goes to the question that matters, which is how to split something, and not to arguing over whether it's a 3 or a 5.

## The data

I wanted more than a feeling that things were better, so I compared 14 sprints before the change with 14 sprints after it. Team size stayed at seven and sprint length stayed at two weeks, so the comparison is fairly clean.

- **Planned work finished:** before, we finished 71% of what we planned in a sprint on average. After, 86%.
- **Median cycle time** (from starting a ticket to merging it): down from 3.4 days to 2.1 days.

Why did this happen? I'll be honest that what follows is a guess. I think small tickets just have fewer ways to go wrong. There's less hidden scope, fewer surprises halfway through and less of "oh, this also touches the sync code." I should also say I didn't measure review time, so I can't tell you whether smaller pull requests got reviewed faster. It seems likely, but I don't have the numbers.

## What got worse

Not everything improved, and this part matters just as much.

Roadmap forecasts got worse. With points, our product manager, Dev Patel, could say a feature was 40 points and fit it into a quarter. You could argue about whether that number meant anything (see Sam's question), but it was a number and people could plan around it.

Now we forecast by counting tickets. That works fine for small and medium features. For big ones it's much rougher, because we don't know how many tickets a big feature will become until we start splitting it, and splitting is exactly the work we put off until the feature is close.

In Q3 this went wrong twice. Two of our five forecasts were off by more than a month:

- **Calendar sync** shipped six weeks late.
- **The notifications rewrite** shipped five weeks late.

Dev tells me he now spends more time explaining forecasts than he used to spend defending a number. That's a real cost and it falls on him, not on the engineers who got shorter meetings. We haven't solved it yet.

## What we'd tell another team

If you're thinking about doing this, here is my honest advice.

It works if your work can be split small. Most of what we build is product software (screens, endpoints, integrations) and almost all of it splits fine once you push on it.

It won't work if you ship big things that can't be divided. Hardware is one example and data migrations are another. If a piece of work only has value once all of it is done, a rule about two-day tickets will just make you pretend.

Also, keep in mind what our evidence is. It's one team over 28 sprints. It is not a study. Our numbers got better, but I can't separate the change in process from everything else that happened this year. Use it as a data point, not proof.

## How we talk about size now

We didn't stop talking about size. We just reduced it to one question: can this be done in two days?

Most of the time the answer is quick and obvious, either yes or "no, split it." The interesting cases are when nobody can answer. We've learned that this usually isn't an estimation problem. It means we don't understand the ticket yet.

That's a more useful thing to find out in planning than whether something is a 5.

**For:** Marc Ellery, VP Customer Success — Leadership review, Friday
**Prepared from:** Priya Nair's analysis notes (9 Oct)

## Recommendation

**Don't commit budget to scaling onboarding calls or rolling out the checklist more widely yet.** Run two short, low-cost tests first, then decide with data on 90-day churn:

1. **Randomized test of onboarding calls.** Offer calls to a random half of new SMB sign-ups and compare 90-day churn against the other half.
2. **Finish measuring the checklist pilot.** Get 90-day churn for the 95 pilot accounts from August. If the data supports it, run a randomized checklist test alongside the calls test.

Then choose between calls, the checklist, or both, based on churn reduced per unit of cost.

## Why

**Accounts with calls churn less, but the calls may not be the cause.**
- 90-day churn for Q2 SMB sign-ups: **11.4%** with an onboarding call (212 accounts) vs **17.9%** without (640 accounts), a 6.5-point gap.
- Calls are opt-in. Accounts that booked a call were already more engaged *before* it happened: 5.1 first-week logins vs 2.3. Part or all of the gap may reflect who signs up for calls, not what the call does.
- Scaling calls is expensive. At about 1.5 CSM hours per call, covering the ~640 accounts per quarter that currently skip calls would take roughly 960 CSM hours per quarter.

**The checklist looks promising, but we haven't measured its effect on churn yet.**
- August pilot (95 accounts, 2 weeks): week-2 activation was **61%** vs **48%** for accounts that signed up in the same weeks without it.
- We have no 90-day churn data for this group yet, so we don't know whether better activation leads to lower churn.
- The checklist is already built (about 3 engineer-weeks), so expanding it would cost little more. That makes it a cheap candidate to test.

## Caveats

- No randomized test of calls has been run. The 6.5-point gap is an association, not a measured effect.
- This analysis covers SMB accounts only. Mid-market and enterprise accounts were not examined.
- Budget has not yet been discussed with Marc. The cost figures above are estimates of effort, not a costed plan.

Approve the two tests above, including a modest CSM time allocation for the calls test. We will bring a scale/no-scale recommendation once the 90-day results come in.

**To:** Dana Okafor, Head of Operations
**Re:** Larkspur vs. Quillon pilot results
**Decision needed by:** 30 April

## Recommendation

**Choose Quillon, but only after it passes a short test at normal load.** Do not sign with either vendor on the pilot data alone.

- Larkspur was tested at normal load and **missed your latency requirement** (310 ms p95 against a 300 ms limit).
- Quillon met both requirements, but **only at about a third of normal load**, during the Easter freeze. That result doesn't tell us how it performs at 40,000 requests per day.

The test would be a Quillon run at or above 40,000 requests per day, for at least 5 to 7 business days, completed before 30 April. If Quillon holds p95 latency at or under 300 ms and on-time delivery at or above 95%, sign with Quillon. If it doesn't, neither vendor has met your requirements, and the decision becomes the trade-off described in "If the Quillon test fails" below.

## Results against your requirements

Requirements: p95 API latency at or under 300 ms at 40,000 requests per day, and on-time delivery of at least 95%.

| | Larkspur | Quillon |
|---|---|---|
| Pilot window | 3–16 Feb (14 days) | 24 Mar–6 Apr (14 days), included the Easter freeze |
| Average volume | 41,000/day (normal) | 14,000/day (about 35% of normal) |
| p95 latency | 310 ms: **fails** (10 ms over) | 240 ms: passes, **but not at normal load** |

## Why the pilot doesn't settle it

1. **The two pilots aren't comparable.** They ran at different times, at different volumes, and never side by side. Latency usually gets worse as load rises, so Quillon's 240 ms at 14,000/day doesn't show it can stay under 300 ms at 40,000/day. The low-volume freeze period may also have made on-time delivery easier.
2. **Larkspur's miss is small but real.** 310 ms is 3% over the limit, measured at the volume we actually run. It fails the requirement as written.

- **Hold off on signing.** Run both vendors side by side at normal load, and accept that the May migration window will slip.

# Post-mortem: Checkout outage, 7 October

**Format:** blameless. This review looks at how our systems and processes let a routine config change become a 49-minute outage. It does not look at who made the change.

## Summary

At 14:02 UTC a config change to the payments service set `payment-timeout` to `null` instead of 30 seconds. In production, payment requests hung until the gateway cut them off at 60 seconds, so checkout failed. The alert fired 7 minutes later. Recovery took another 42 minutes because of how our paging works and because the rollback runbook was out of date. Error rates were back under 1% at 14:51.

## Impact

| | |
|---|---|
| Duration | 49 minutes (14:02–14:51 UTC) |
| Failed checkouts | ~3,100 |
| Peak checkout error rate | 38% |
| Mitigating factor | Happened outside the evening peak, at about half of peak volume |

If this had happened at peak, the number of failed checkouts would probably have been about double. [Inference: assumes failures scale with traffic.]

## Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event | Gap |
|---|---|---|
| 14:02 | Config change to the payments service deployed by the on-call engineer | |
| 14:09 | Error-rate alert fires. The page goes to the primary on-call only | 7 min to detect |
| 14:21 | Primary acknowledges the page | 12 min to acknowledge |
| 14:34 | Rollback starts | 13 min to diagnose and decide |
| 14:51 | Error rate back under 1% | 17 min to roll back |

## What happened

### 1. A harmful value passed every check

- The config schema accepts `null` for `payment-timeout`.
- Staging falls back to a default when the value is null, so staging validation passed.
- Production has no default. Requests waited until the gateway's 60-second cutoff and then failed.

Staging and production handle missing config differently, so a passing staging check told us nothing about production behaviour for this field. Any engineer pushing this change would have seen the same green checks.

### 2. Detection took 7 minutes

The error-rate alert fired 7 minutes after the change. **We don't yet know why.** Possible causes include the alert's evaluation window or threshold, and the fact that each request took 60 seconds to fail. This has not been investigated.

### 3. One person was paged, with a 30-minute fallback

The policy sends each page to one person. The secondary is paged only if the page goes unacknowledged for 30 minutes. That makes one person a single point of failure for up to half an hour of customer impact.

The secondary on-call was in mandatory security training from 14:00. That training was scheduled by the company. On-call engineers being in required meetings is predictable, and a paging policy has to work anyway.

> **Discrepancy in the notes:** the incident notes say the secondary "never saw the escalation." Under the policy described, the secondary would only have been paged at about 14:39 (30 minutes after 14:09). The primary acknowledged at 14:21, so no escalation should have been sent at all. We need to confirm with the paging tool's logs whether the secondary was actually paged.

### 4. The rollback runbook was out of date

The rollback runbook was written before we moved to the new deploy tool. Responders had to find the right steps on the old wiki, and the rollback took 17 minutes. Undoing a one-field config change should take a few minutes.

## What went well

- Once the rollback started, it fully restored service, and the error rate went back under 1%.
- The error-rate alert did fire, even if it was slow.

## Action items

| # | Action | Addresses |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Make `payment-timeout` non-nullable in the config schema, and check other fields that accept null | Bad value passing validation |
| 2 | Make staging fail, not fall back, when a value is missing, so it behaves like production (or give production the same explicit default) | Staging/production mismatch |
| 3 | Find out why the alert took 7 minutes, and tune its window or threshold | Slow detection |
| 4 | Cut the secondary escalation from 30 minutes to about 5, or page primary and secondary together for checkout-impacting alerts | Single point of failure |
| 5 | Treat mandatory training and meetings as on-call conflicts: hand over cover in advance | Predictable unavailability |
| 6 | Rewrite the rollback runbook for the current deploy tool, and test it with a drill | Slow rollback |
| 7 | Check all runbooks that refer to the old deploy tool | Same class of staleness |
| 8 | Check paging-tool logs to find out whether the secondary was paged | Discrepancy in the notes |

Owners and dates to be assigned after the all-hands.

## Open questions

- Why did the alert take 7 minutes to fire?
- Was the secondary actually paged, and if so, when?
- What took the 13 minutes between acknowledging the page and starting the rollback (diagnosis, finding the runbook, something else)? The notes don't say.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""csvtrim: strip spaces around every field of a CSV file and drop blank rows.

Standard library only. Tested with Python 3.11.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import sys


def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        prog="csvtrim",
        description="Strip spaces around every field and drop rows that are empty.",
    )
    parser.add_argument("-i", "--input", required=True, help="CSV file to read (UTF-8, comma-separated)")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", help="file to write; default is standard output")
    parser.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="print row counts to standard error")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    try:
        src = open(args.input, newline="", encoding="utf-8")
    except OSError as exc:
        print(f"csvtrim: cannot read {args.input}: {exc.strerror}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    dst = open(args.output, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") if args.output else sys.stdout
    kept = dropped = 0
    with src:
        writer = csv.writer(dst)
        for row in csv.reader(src):
            cells = [cell.strip() for cell in row]
            if not any(cells):
                dropped += 1
                continue
            writer.writerow(cells)
            kept += 1
    if args.output:
        dst.close()

    if args.verbose:
        print(f"kept {kept} rows, dropped {dropped} blank rows", file=sys.stderr)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# csvtrim

Strip leading/trailing whitespace from every field of a CSV file and drop rows that are entirely blank.

Single script, Python standard library only. Tested with Python 3.11.

## Usage

```sh
python3 csvtrim.py -i INPUT [-o OUTPUT] [-v]
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-i`, `--input` | CSV file to read (required). UTF-8, comma-separated. |
| `-o`, `--output` | File to write. Defaults to standard output. Overwritten if it exists. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print kept/dropped row counts to standard error. |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help. |

## Examples

```sh
# Clean a file into a new file, with a summary
python3 csvtrim.py -i raw.csv -o clean.csv -v
# stderr: kept 120 rows, dropped 3 blank rows

# Write to stdout and pipe onward
python3 csvtrim.py -i raw.csv | head
```

Input:

```csv
 name , city
  Ana ,  Lisbon

 , 
Bo,Oslo
```

Output:

```csv
name,city
Ana,Lisbon
Bo,Oslo
```

## Behavior

- Every field is trimmed with Python's `str.strip()`, so tabs and other whitespace are removed too, not only spaces. Whitespace inside a field is kept.
- A row is dropped if all its fields are empty after trimming (including fully empty lines).
- The header row is treated like any other row.
- Quoting follows Python's `csv` module defaults: quoted fields are parsed correctly, and output is re-quoted only where needed. Original quoting style is not preserved.
- Output is UTF-8. A UTF-8 BOM in the input is not removed and will stay attached to the first field.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |

# csvtrim

`csvtrim` cleans up a CSV file. It removes leading and trailing whitespace from every field and drops rows where every field is empty after trimming.

It is a single Python script that uses only the standard library. It has been tested with Python 3.11.

## Quick start

From the directory that contains `csvtrim.py`, run it on the bundled `sample.csv`:

```sh
python3 csvtrim.py -i sample.csv -v
```

Output:

```text
id,name,qty
1,Linh,4
2,Minh,7
3,An,2
kept 4 rows, dropped 2 blank rows
```

The cleaned CSV is written to standard output. The `kept … dropped …` line comes from `-v` and is written to standard error.

To write the result to a file instead:

```sh
python3 csvtrim.py -i sample.csv -o cleaned.csv
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-i`, `--input FILE` | Required. CSV file to read. Must be UTF-8 and comma-separated. |
| `-o`, `--output FILE` | File to write. If omitted, output goes to standard output. An existing file is overwritten. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print the number of kept and dropped rows to standard error. |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show usage and exit. |

## Behaviour

- Each field is trimmed with Python's `str.strip()`. This removes spaces, tabs and other whitespace at the start and end of a field. Whitespace inside a field is left as is.
- A row is dropped if all of its fields are empty after trimming. This includes empty lines and rows such as `,,` or `  ,  ,  `.
- The header row is treated like any other row: it is trimmed, and it is kept unless it is blank.
- Output is UTF-8 CSV written by Python's `csv` module with its default settings. Fields are quoted only when needed, and lines end with `\r\n`.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `0` | Success. |
| `1` | The input file could not be opened. A message such as `csvtrim: cannot read data.csv: No such file or directory` is printed to standard error. |
| `2` | Invalid command-line arguments, for example a missing `-i`. |

Other errors, such as an input file that is not valid UTF-8 or an output path that cannot be written, end with a Python traceback.

"""tailr: print lines from a log file, optionally following it as it grows.

Needs Python 3.11 or newer (tomllib).
"""
import argparse
import re
import sys
import time
import tomllib
from datetime import datetime

DEFAULTS = {
    "pattern": "",
    "follow": True,
    "poll_interval_ms": 250,
    "max_line_bytes": 8192,
    "color": "auto",
    "timestamp_format": "",
    "output_file": "",
}


def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="tailr", description="Print and follow log lines.")
    parser.add_argument("--config", default="tailr.toml", help="TOML config file (default: tailr.toml)")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    with open(args.config, "rb") as fh:
        cfg = {**DEFAULTS, **tomllib.load(fh)}
    if "path" not in cfg:
        print("tailr: the config has no 'path'", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    rx = re.compile(cfg["pattern"]) if cfg["pattern"] else None
    colour = cfg["color"] == "always" or (cfg["color"] == "auto" and sys.stdout.isatty())
    extra = open(cfg["output_file"], "a", encoding="utf-8") if cfg["output_file"] else None
    print(f"tailr: watching {cfg['path']}", file=sys.stderr)

    with open(cfg["path"], "rb") as log:
        while True:
            raw = log.readline()
            if not raw:
                if not cfg["follow"]:
                    break
                time.sleep(cfg["poll_interval_ms"] / 1000)
                continue
            line = raw.decode("utf-8", errors="replace").rstrip("\n")
            if len(raw) > cfg["max_line_bytes"]:
                line = raw[: cfg["max_line_bytes"]].decode("utf-8", errors="ignore") + "..."
            if rx and not rx.search(line):
                continue
            if colour and rx:
                line = rx.sub(lambda m: f"\x1b[1m{m.group(0)}\x1b[0m", line)
            if cfg["timestamp_format"]:
                line = datetime.now().strftime(cfg["timestamp_format"]) + line
            print(line)
            if extra:
                extra.write(line + "\n")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Getting started with tailr

tailr prints the lines of a log file and can keep following the file as new lines are written. You can filter lines with a regular expression, highlight the matches, add a timestamp to each line, and copy the output to a second file.

## Requirements

- Python 3.11 or newer. tailr uses `tomllib`, which was added in 3.11.
- No third-party packages.

## Quick start

1. Copy the example config:

   ```sh
   cp tailr.toml.example tailr.toml
   ```

2. Set `path` in `tailr.toml` to the log you want to watch:

   ```toml
   path = "/var/log/app.log"
   ```

3. Run tailr:

   ```sh
   python3 tailr.py
   ```

   tailr writes `tailr: watching /var/log/app.log` to stderr and then prints the log lines to stdout. Press `Ctrl+C` to stop.

To use a config file somewhere else, pass `--config`:

```sh
python3 tailr.py --config /etc/tailr/app.toml
```

The only command-line option is `--config`. Every other setting goes in the config file.

## Things to know

- **tailr starts at the top of the file.** It prints the whole file first and then waits for new lines. It does not start at the end like `tail -f`. On a large log, this first pass can print a lot.
- **Stopping:** if `follow = true` (the default), tailr runs until you press `Ctrl+C`. If `follow = false`, it exits when it reaches the end of the file.
- **Exit codes:** `0` means a normal finish (only possible when `follow = false`). `2` means the config has no `path`. If the config file or the log file can't be opened, or `pattern` is not a valid regex, tailr exits with a Python traceback.
- **Unknown keys are ignored.** A misspelled key, such as `colour` instead of `color`, gives no warning, and the default value is used.
- **Log rotation is not handled.** If the log is rotated or truncated, tailr keeps reading the old file handle.

## Configuration reference

The config is a TOML file, `tailr.toml` by default. Only `path` is required. Any key you leave out uses its default.

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | *(required)* | The log file to read. |
| `pattern` | string (regex) | `""` | Print only lines that match this Python regular expression (`re.search`, so it can match anywhere in the line). `""` prints every line. |
| `follow` | bool | `true` | After reaching the end of the file, keep checking for new lines. If `false`, exit at the end of the file. |
| `poll_interval_ms` | integer | `250` | How long to wait between checks for new data, in milliseconds. Only used when `follow = true`. The example config gives a range of 50–5000, but tailr does not check it, so keep your value inside that range. |
| `max_line_bytes` | integer | `8192` | Lines longer than this are cut to this many bytes and end with `...`. The trailing newline counts toward the limit, and the cut happens before `pattern` is applied, so text after the cut can't match. |
| `color` | string | `"auto"` | Highlights pattern matches in bold. `"always"` always highlights. `"auto"` highlights only when stdout is a terminal. `"never"` or any other value turns highlighting off. Has no effect when `pattern` is empty. |
| `timestamp_format` | string | `""` | A [`strftime`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-and-strptime-format-codes) format added in front of each printed line. It shows the time tailr printed the line, not the time in the log entry. No separator is added, so include one yourself, for example `"%H:%M:%S "`. `""` means no prefix. |
| `output_file` | string | `""` | Also append each printed line to this file (UTF-8). The file is created if it doesn't exist. `""` means no copy. The copy is exactly what was printed, timestamp and color codes included, so use `color = "auto"` or `"never"` if you want a clean file. |

Lines are read as UTF-8. Invalid bytes are replaced with `�`.

## Examples

Show only errors and warnings, with a time prefix:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
pattern = "ERROR|WARN"
timestamp_format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S "
```

Scan a file once and save the matching lines:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
pattern = "timeout"
follow = false
color = "never"
output_file = "timeouts.txt"
```

Follow a busy log and check for new lines more often:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
poll_interval_ms = 50
```

# Getting started with tailr

tailr prints the lines of a log file and, by default, keeps watching the file and prints new lines as they are written. Everything is set in a TOML config file.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer (tailr uses the standard-library `tomllib`). No other packages.

## Quick start

1. Copy the example config:

   ```sh
   cp tailr.toml.example tailr.toml
   ```

2. Set `path` in `tailr.toml` to the log you want to watch:

   ```toml
   path = "/var/log/app.log"
   ```

3. Run tailr:

   ```sh
   python tailr.py
   ```

   tailr prints `tailr: watching /var/log/app.log` to stderr, then the log lines to stdout. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

To use a config file somewhere else:

```sh
python tailr.py --config /etc/tailr/app.toml
```

`--config` is the only command-line option. Its default is `tailr.toml` in the current directory.

## What to expect

- **tailr starts at the beginning of the file**, not the end. On a large log, it prints the whole file first, then follows new lines.
- With `follow = false`, it prints the file once and exits.
- It does not detect log rotation or truncation: if the file is replaced, tailr keeps reading the old one.
- Invalid UTF-8 is shown with the replacement character (�) instead of failing.

## Common setups

Show only errors and highlight the match:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
pattern = "ERROR|FATAL"
color = "always"
```

Print the file once (like `cat`, filtered) and exit:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
pattern = "timeout"
follow = false
```

Add a time prefix and keep a copy of what was printed:

```toml
path = "/var/log/app.log"
timestamp_format = "[%H:%M:%S] "
output_file = "/tmp/tailr-copy.log"
```

## Config reference

Only `path` is required. Any option you leave out uses its default.

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | none (required) | File to read. |
| `pattern` | string (regex) | `""` | Print only lines that match this Python regular expression (searched anywhere in the line). Empty prints every line. |
| `follow` | bool | `true` | Keep waiting for new lines after reaching the end of the file. `false` exits at end of file. |
| `poll_interval_ms` | integer | `250` | How long to wait, in milliseconds, before checking the file again for new data. The example file recommends 50–5000; tailr does not enforce this range. |
| `max_line_bytes` | integer | `8192` | Lines longer than this are cut to this many bytes and end with `...`. The length counted includes the trailing newline. |
| `color` | string | `"auto"` | Bold-highlight the parts matching `pattern`. `"always"` highlights, `"never"` does not, `"auto"` highlights only when stdout is a terminal. Has no effect without `pattern`. Any other value acts like `"never"`. |
| `timestamp_format` | string | `""` | [strftime](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#strftime-and-strptime-format-codes) format added in front of each printed line. It is the time tailr printed the line, not the time in the log. No space is added, so include one yourself (e.g. `"%H:%M:%S "`). Empty means no prefix. |
| `output_file` | string | `""` | Also append every printed line to this file. Lines are written exactly as printed, including the timestamp prefix and, if highlighting is on, the color escape codes. Empty means no file. |

Unknown keys are ignored without a warning, so check spelling if an option seems to have no effect.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `tailr: the config has no 'path'`, exit code 2 | Add `path` to the config. |
| `FileNotFoundError` traceback at start | The config file (default `tailr.toml` in the current directory) or the `path` file does not exist. |
| `re.error` traceback at start | `pattern` is not a valid regular expression. In TOML basic strings, escape backslashes (`"\\d+"`) or use single quotes (`'\d+'`). |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tomllib'` | Python is older than 3.11. |
| Strange `^[[1m` characters in `output_file` | `color = "always"` writes escape codes into the file too. Use `"auto"` or `"never"`. |

# Cap retry backoff delay with `max_delay`

Fixes #412.

## Why

Last week in staging, the upstream was down and one job slept for 17 minutes between retries. `backoff_delays` doubled the delay on every attempt with no upper limit.

## What changed

- `taskrunner/retry.py`: `backoff_delays` takes a new `max_delay` parameter, defaulting to `30.0` seconds. Each delay is capped at `max_delay` before jitter is added, so the real sleep can go up to `max_delay + jitter` (30.1 s with the defaults).
- `max_delay=None` turns the cap off and gives the old uncapped behaviour.
- `tests/test_retry.py`: two new tests:
  - `test_delay_is_capped`: with 10 attempts, no delay goes above 30.0.
  - `test_max_delay_none_is_uncapped`: with `max_delay=None`, the 10th delay is 512.0.

## Behaviour change

The cap is on by default, so every existing caller is now limited to 30 s between retries unless it passes `max_delay=None`. The nightly sync is the one that matters: it uses `attempts=12`, so its later retries used to wait several minutes and now wait about 30 s. This is intended, but it changes how that job runs.

## Testing

- `pytest tests/test_retry.py` run locally: 4 passed.
- I have not run the full test suite, and CI has not run yet.

## Not included

- No design doc.
- README and docs are unchanged. The new parameter is described only in the docstring.

Research statement, para 2 (current work). Postdoc at the Halden Institute for Maritime History (2 yrs). They want "what you've done, why it matters, where it goes". ~140 words. Keep it concise and tell the story of what I did. -- Dalia

PhD (Aug 2021 - Jun 2025). Corpus: 412 ship's logbooks, Brightwater Company archive, 1790-1840. 19 have no date at all (cover lost / pages rebound). Dating by hand = how archivists did it, slow, by eye.
Attempt 1: classify the pages directly from 14 letterform measures (slant, x-height ratio, 'st' ligature, long-s...). SVM got 71% right decade; random forest 78%. Looked ok, but it was dating the page and kept confusing neighbouring decades. 
Attempt 2 (dead end): paper watermarks. ~60% of logs rebound later; useless. Also tried automatic HTR on the logs, character error 23%, dropped.
THE TURN: stop dating pages, date scribes. 6 main hands (H1-H6) write 83% of all logs. Payroll book PB-1802 gives start/leave years for clerks, so each hand has a tenure window. Date the hand, then the log inherits the window. 
Result: 17 of 19 undated logs now sit in a ~10-year window (+-5). 2 still ambiguous: H4 and H5 overlap 1811-1816.
Checked on the 60 logs where date known (held out): 54 right (90%).
Next (postdoc): Corvane Company archive, ~900 logs; test whether the tenure-window idea transfers when no payroll book survives. Collaboration idea with archivist Priya Nand (Corvane). Also fix the H4/H5 overlap via ink analysis? maybe.
Hours spent: 3 yrs of transcribing, don't mention. Supervisor Prof. Aldous Weir.

My doctoral work began as a quarrel with the map. The county's tithe maps for 1840 show field boundaries that the surveyors of the 1880s could no longer find, and historians had treated the gap as carelessness. I thought it was evidence. By laying 212 parish maps over one another, I found that the missing boundaries cluster around enclosures agreed by private act, which the tithe clerks recorded and the later surveyors did not. The lost fields were a trail, not an error.

That changed my question from where the boundaries went to who stopped writing them down. In the second half of the thesis I follow the clerks themselves, asking how a record that looks neutral was shaped by a few people's habits. At Halden I want to take that question to a larger and messier archive: first at the harbour, then along the coast.

| Cost per ticket | $14.20 | $9.80 | −31% |
| Tickets handled per agent per day | 17 | 26 | +53% |

The "after" figures cover only one month, and part of that month was hypercare. They show the direction of change but do not yet prove the desk will hold these levels. The weekly KPI report (Section 8) should confirm whether the gains last.

## 6. Delivery highlights

- **Data migration.** Datamove Ltd migrated 38,500 tickets on a fixed price and removed 2,300 duplicates from the South export. Limiting the migration to 24 months of tickets (decided 17 February) kept the work to that size.
- **Phone integration.** Owned by Pavel Novak, built from 6 April for the 22 June go-live. Its purpose is to stop agents logging South desk phone contacts by hand.
- **People and adoption.** Some South desk agents preferred the old tool (risk raised 19 May). Pavel Novak ran two extra training sessions, and the lessons-learned workshop found that these removed most of the resistance before go-live.
- **Hypercare.** In four weeks (22 June – 17 July) the team logged 126 migration-related issues and closed 124 of them.
- **Handover.** The runbook went to operations (Nadia Haddad). Agent accounts and permissions were audited, and the final vendor invoice was approved (Karl Osei).

## 7. Change control

There was one approved change request during the project.

| CR | Raised | Approved | Change | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CR-03 Phone integration | 3 Mar 2026, Pavel Novak | 5 Mar 2026, Sofia Marin | Add phone integration to Deskwise | +$7,000 budget (to $92,000); go-live 1 Jun → 22 Jun |

CR-03 was raised because about a third of South desk contacts come in by phone, and nobody had asked about phone contacts during requirements. The project team supported the change on 3 March.

## 8. Open items and decisions requested

Status as of 5 August 2026. Please confirm these items are resolved, or assign them, before you sign off closure.

| # | Item | Status | Decision requested |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Decommission the legacy North and South ticket systems | No date, no owner | Assign an owner and a decommission date. Until then the organisation runs and pays for three ticket systems. Older tickets remain in the legacy archives, so decide where they will be kept. |
| 2 | Weekly KPI report to operations | Format agreed, no owner | Assign an owner so that the July results in Section 5 are tracked over time. |
| 3 | 2 open hypercare issues | Open at hypercare close | Confirm that operations has taken ownership of them. |
| 4 | Formal project closure | Planned 31 July; not signed off | Sign off closure once items 1–3 have owners. |

## 9. Lessons learned

These come from the team workshop of 24 July 2026 (Karl Osei, Nadia Haddad, Pavel Novak, Ines Duarte).

**What worked**

- Migrating only the last 24 months of tickets kept the migration manageable at 38,500 tickets.
- Extra training for the South desk, agreed early (19 May), dealt with resistance before go-live.
- A defined four-week hypercare period closed 124 of 126 issues.

**What did not work**

- Phone integration arrived late through CR-03. It cost $7,000 and three weeks, and then overran by $900. Requirements had not asked which contact channels the desks use.
- The South export contained 2,300 duplicate tickets, and this was found after the migration window had been set.

**Recommendations for future projects**

1. Freeze scope before the plan is baselined, and ask explicitly about every contact channel (phone, chat, email) during requirements.
2. Sample each source system for data quality before agreeing a migration date.
3. Name owners for decommissioning and for post-go-live reporting in the plan itself, not at handover.

The figures in this report come from the project folder: the kickoff notes (12 Jan), project meeting notes (17 Feb, 3 Mar, 14 Apr, 19 May), plan v1 and plan v2 FINAL, CR-03, the final budget, the Datamove final invoice, the KPI before/after file, the lessons-learned notes and the handover checklist.
